screens.title: BGP Path Attributes and Best Path Selection
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how BGP decides which route is best and which attributes you can change to shape traffic. BGP is the protocol that governs how autonomous systems exchange reachability; it does not rely on a single numeric metric like many interior protocols. Instead, it evaluates a sequence of path attributes — including weight, local preference, AS path, origin, MED, and communities — to make deterministic decisions. You'll see that some attributes are local to a router, some are shared inside an AS, and others are exchanged between ASes. This distinction matters because it determines whether you can influence outbound traffic from your AS, or inbound traffic seen by your peers. Concrete examples in the chapter show using a neighbor weight, setting local preference via a route-map, and AS path prepending to alter how an upstream ISP prefers your routes. We'll also cover the exact order BGP evaluates attributes so you avoid common mistakes, like attempting to use MED when local preference already resolved the choice. By the end you'll be able to explain the evaluation order, apply route-maps to set attributes, and reason about the impact of changes on inter-domain routing. Consider how a single attribute change could make a backup link carry all traffic — that's why careful testing matters. Why might you prefer local preference over AS path prepending for outbound traffic control? We'll explore that in detail.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › BGP Path Attributes
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

BGP Path Attributes and Best Path Selection

Understand attribute scope, how the algorithm evaluates them, and how to use route-maps safely to influence traffic.

Attribute scope
Local vs iBGP vs eBGP
Why this chapter matters

Small attribute changes can flip traffic paths across your network or across providers. Knowing the algorithm order prevents ineffective changes and outages.

In this lesson
Attributes, order, route-maps, troubleshooting
Explore Key Topics
Weight
Router-local influence for outbound path selection at the speaker.
Local Preference
iBGP-wide preference shaping which exit an AS uses for outbound traffic.
AS_Path & PREPEND
Change how peers view your distance to influence inbound traffic.
Visual Concept
Scope map
Weight: local · LocalPref: iBGP · AS_Path/MED/Community: eBGP
Order matters
An early attribute will trump changes made later in evaluation.
Quick start
Start by listing attributes for a prefix with the show ip bgp commands. Identify which attribute you can change safely and test in a lab before you apply to production.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives are designed so you can both explain and act on BGP path behavior. First, you'll identify key BGP path attributes — weight, local preference, AS path, origin, MED, and community — and explain where each one applies. That means distinguishing router-local attributes from those exchanged inside an AS, and those sent between ASes. Second, you'll describe the BGP best path selection algorithm as an ordered decision process so you can predict which attribute will win when two policies conflict. Third, you'll set and test attributes using route-maps to influence outbound and inbound traffic, including configuring neighbor weight and local-preference and performing AS path prepending. Finally, you'll reason about the operational implications and troubleshoot common selection issues using the show ip bgp commands. Each objective combines conceptual knowledge and lab actions so you can prove competency. For example, after learning to set local preference with a route-map you'll test outbound path selection and verify that all iBGP speakers pick the configured exit. Keep in mind that manipulating attributes has safety implications; always validate in a controlled environment and document changes before applying to production.

screens.title: Weight — Cisco-proprietary, Router-local Influence
screens.narratorSegment: Weight is a Cisco-proprietary attribute that exists only on the local router and is the first criterion in BGP's best path selection. Because weight is evaluated before every other attribute, setting a higher weight on a route immediately makes the local router prefer that route for outbound traffic. This makes weight ideal for quick, per-router overrides where you want a specific speaker to use a chosen exit without affecting other iBGP peers. You can configure weight directly with a neighbor statement or set it in a route-map. For example, using neighbor 10.0.0.2 weight 200 makes routes from that neighbor preferred locally. Alternatively, a route-map applied inbound can match specific prefixes and set weight values selectively. A concrete use case is when a router has two eBGP neighbors and you need one router to prefer the lower-cost link for certain prefixes while leaving other routers unchanged. A common misconception is to use weight when you mean to influence the entire AS; remember weight does not propagate, so it will not change decisions on other routers. Key verification steps are to run show ip bgp for the prefix on the router and observe the weight value and the selected route. Always document weight changes and test in lab because local overrides can cause asymmetric flows that complicate troubleshooting.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Weight
Definition and scope

Weight is local to the router and is evaluated first by BGP. It does not get advertised to neighbors and only affects the local best-path choice.

Configuration example
neighbor 10.0.0.2 weight 200
!
route-map SET_WEIGHT permit 10
 set weight 300
!
neighbor 10.0.0.3 route-map SET_WEIGHT in
Example
Make R1 prefer R2 for a prefix by setting neighbor weight on R1. This affects only R1.
Common mistake
Expecting weight to change decisions on other iBGP speakers. It will not — use local-preference for AS-wide influence.
Read and verify

After configuration, run show ip bgp <prefix> to verify the weight field and confirm the selected path. Record before and after to ensure expected behavior.

Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Weight is the fastest way to force a single router to choose a route. It wins early and does not propagate.

screens.title: Local Preference — Influence Across the AS
screens.narratorSegment: Local Preference is a well-known, discretionary attribute that iBGP peers exchange inside an autonomous system. It is evaluated after weight but before AS path, so setting a higher local preference on routes learned from a chosen neighbor causes all iBGP speakers to prefer that exit for outbound traffic. This makes local preference the primary tool when you want entire AS behavior to change, unlike weight which only affects a single router. Typically you set local preference using a route-map applied on inbound neighbor sessions, for example set local-preference 200 for prefixes learned from your preferred upstream. A concrete scenario: if Router A should be the primary exit for 1.1.1.0/24, configure the neighbor connected to Router A to set local preference higher than default 100. Verification involves running show ip bgp for the prefix on multiple iBGP speakers and confirming the local-preference value and that the chosen next-hop aligns with your desired exit. A common misconception is to rely on AS path for outbound control; AS path affects how other ASes prefer your routes for inbound traffic, not how your AS chooses its own exit. Use local preference for AS-wide outbound policy and document the policy so operators understand global path preferences.

keyIdea.text: Use local preference for consistent, AS-wide outbound exit selection; set via route-maps and verify across iBGP speakers.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Local Preference
What it is and why to use it

Local preference is propagated to all iBGP peers and instructs every speaker which path to prefer for outbound traffic. Change it when you want AS-wide behavior to shift.

Route-map example
route-map SET_LOCAL_PREF permit 10
 set local-preference 200
!
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 10.0.0.2 remote-as 65002
 neighbor 10.0.0.2 route-map SET_LOCAL_PREF in
Example
Prefer R2 for outbound 1.1.1.0/24 by applying a higher local preference on routes learned from R2.
Misconception
Do not expect local preference to affect how other ASes send traffic to you — that is AS path or community work.
Verify and document

After setting local preference, check multiple iBGP routers to confirm they all chose the intended exit. Use show ip bgp <prefix> and compare local-preference fields across speakers.

Key Takeaway

Local Preference is your AS-wide knob for outbound traffic. Apply it consistently and verify across iBGP peers.

screens.title: AS_Path and Prepending — Influence Inbound Traffic
screens.narratorSegment: AS_Path is a list of autonomous system numbers a route has traversed and is central to how remote ASes decide where to send traffic to you. BGP prefers shorter AS paths, so adding your AS number multiple times — prepending — makes your route appear longer and therefore less preferred by upstream peers. This is the standard operational method to influence inbound traffic without asking your peers to change their policies. For example, if Router Y should be a backup for 203.0.113.0/24, configure Router Y to prepend its AS number two or three times before advertising the prefix to the ISP. The chapter example shows a route-map PREPEND_AS with set as-path prepend 65002 65002 65002 applied outbound. After changes, verify on your peer with show ip bgp that the AS_Path length increased. A common trap is over-prepending: if you add too many AS numbers you may make the route unreachable or cause unexpected failover to a longer but stable path. Also remember AS path only affects other ASes' inbound decisions — it will not change your own AS outbound choices. Think of AS path as advertising a longer road to make others choose a different entrance to reach you.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › AS_Path & Prepending
How AS_Path works

AS_Path is examined to prefer shorter sequences of AS numbers. It represents the external distance to a prefix and is visible to other ASes.

Prepend example
route-map PREPEND_AS permit 10
 set as-path prepend 65002 65002 65002
!
neighbor 10.0.0.1 route-map PREPEND_AS out
Operational example
Make a data center link appear farther away to the ISP so the ISP sends traffic to the primary data center instead.
Verification and cautions

After prepending, use show ip bgp <prefix> on the peer to confirm the AS_Path includes the extra numbers. Avoid excessive prepending and test failover behavior in a lab.

Key Takeaway

AS_Path prepending is the main tool for inbound shaping; it changes how remote ASes perceive your distance.

screens.title: Origin and MED — Route Source and Inter-AS Entry Preference
screens.narratorSegment: Origin and MED are attributes that come after AS path in the selection sequence and provide additional tie-breaking information. Origin indicates how the route entered BGP: IGP (marked i) for routes injected via the network command, EGP (deprecated), or Incomplete (?) for redistributed routes. Origin is preferred in the order IGP > EGP > Incomplete, so prefer declaring routes via network where possible to give them higher origin preference. MED, or Multi-Exit Discriminator, is an optional attribute that suggests to a neighboring AS which entry point into your AS it should prefer; lower MED is better. Important nuance: MED comparisons are only meaningful when comparing routes received from the same neighboring AS. If you set MED on routes learned from different ASes, BGP will not compare them unless additional configuration is present. A common mistake is to set MED expecting to influence decisions across different upstreams — because MED is evaluated later and constrained by source neighbor, it often has no effect. Use MED when you and a peer have multiple peering points and you want to influence which of your links they will choose. Verify MED values appearing in show ip bgp output and confirm whether routes compared come from the same neighbor.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Origin & MED
Origin attribute

Origin shows how a route entered BGP: IGP (i), EGP (e), or Incomplete (?). IGP is preferred over EGP and Incomplete during comparison.

Practical note
Prefer injecting important prefixes via network or origin protocols to give them better origin preference than redistributed routes.
MED (Multi-Exit Discriminator)

MED suggests to a neighboring AS which of your multiple entry points it should prefer. Lower MED is preferred but comparisons are only done for routes from the same neighboring AS.

When to use MED
When you and a peer have multiple connections and you want to hint which entry they should use.
Pitfall
Expecting MED to influence choices across different neighboring ASes — MED only compares within the same neighbor by default.
Key Takeaway

Use origin to mark route source and MED to advise a neighbor on preferred entry, but respect MED's neighbor scope.

screens.title: Community — Grouping Routes for Policy
screens.narratorSegment: BGP community is an optional, transitive attribute used to tag routes so receiving ASes can apply consistent policies. Communities themselves are not part of the core best-path decision sequence, but they are powerful policy levers. Common communities like no-export or no-advertise control where a route is propagated, and custom communities let you mark prefixes for actions such as prepending, blackholing, or special handling by transit partners. For example, you might tag certain prefixes with a community that instructs an upstream to prefer a particular POP or to avoid advertising the prefix beyond their network. Because communities travel across AS boundaries when transitive, they enable coordination between you and your providers. A misconception is assuming communities automatically change route preference; they only carry labels. The peer must be configured to act on those communities. Use route-maps to set communities with set community and document the semantics you expect from each peer. Verify community propagation via show ip bgp and by asking a cooperative peer to confirm the received community tags in their BGP table. Communities are a policy language — use them to make complex operator intent explicit and automatable.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Community
What communities do

Communities allow you to mark routes with metadata that peers can interpret to apply routing policies, filtering, or transformations.

Route-map example
route-map SET_COMMUNITY permit 10
 set community 65001:100
!
neighbor 10.0.0.1 route-map SET_COMMUNITY out
Example usage
Tag a set of prefixes so an upstream selectively applies prepending or avoids advertising them to a specific region.
Operational notes
  • Communities are labels; peers must honor them by policy.
  • Document community semantics in peering agreements.
  • Use well-known communities like no-export when appropriate.
Key Takeaway

Communities enable coordinated policy and automation across AS boundaries, but they require peer support to have effect.

screens.title: BGP Best Path Selection Algorithm
screens.narratorSegment: The BGP best path selection algorithm is a strict, ordered list of checks that BGP uses to select one best path among many. Understanding the sequence is essential so you apply the correct attribute when you want to influence selection. The sequence begins with weight — the Cisco-local override — followed by local preference for AS-wide decisions. Next, routes that were originated locally via network or redistribute are preferred. Then BGP considers AS_Path length, favoring the shortest list of AS numbers. After AS path, Origin preference is evaluated with IGP preferred over EGP and Incomplete. MED comes next, but MED is only compared when competing routes come from the same neighbor AS. If still tied, eBGP-learned routes are preferred over iBGP, then the lowest IGP metric to the BGP next-hop. For ties among eBGP routes, BGP prefers the oldest route for stability, then breaks remaining ties using the lowest BGP router ID and finally the lowest neighbor IP address. A common troubleshooting mistake is attempting to change a late-stage attribute like MED when an earlier attribute already decided the winner. When you troubleshoot, gather the full path list with show ip bgp <prefix> longer-prefixes and examine each attribute in the precise order above. This lets you reason why one path was chosen and which attribute you need to change to get a different outcome.

keyIdea.title: Algorithm takeaway

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Best Path Algorithm
Selection order (summary)
  1. Weight
  2. Local Preference
  3. Locally originated
  4. AS_Path (shorter)
  5. Origin (IGP > EGP > Incomplete)
  6. MED (lower, same neighbor AS only)
  7. eBGP over iBGP
  8. Lowest IGP metric to next-hop
  9. Oldest eBGP route
  10. Lowest Router ID
  11. Lowest neighbor IP
Process note
When adjusting policies, pick the earliest attribute possible to achieve your goal. That ensures predictable results.
Example diagnosis

If a path you expected to win does not, list all candidate paths with show ip bgp <prefix> and compare attributes in the algorithm order. You may find a higher local-preference or weight decided the outcome before MED or AS path could matter.

Check your understanding
If Local Preference differs between two paths, will AS_Path or MED ever change the selection? No — Local Preference wins earlier in the list.
Key Takeaway

Follow the algorithm order when designing policies and troubleshooting; resolving the earliest decisive attribute yields reliable behavior.

screens.title: Manipulating Attributes with Route-maps
screens.narratorSegment: Route-maps are the practical mechanism for setting BGP attributes in real networks. They let you match prefixes and set attributes like weight, local preference, AS path prepend, MED, or community before the route enters or leaves a BGP session. In the chapter we show examples such as route-map SET_LOCAL_PREF permit 10 with set local-preference 200 applied inbound on a neighbor to prefer that path across the AS. Another example is PREPEND_AS to set as-path prepend 65002 65002 65002 before advertising out to a peer. For weight, you can either use a neighbor weight command for simple cases or set weight in a route-map when you need prefix-level control. Best practice is to document the intent in the route-map and test changes in a lab. Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Route-map Examples
Examples shown in chapter
! Set Local Preference
route-map SET_LOCAL_PREF permit 10
 set local-preference 200
!
neighbor 10.0.0.2 route-map SET_LOCAL_PREF in

!

Practical verification
  1. Capture current show ip bgp <prefix> output.
  2. Apply route-map to neighbor in a lab or maintenance window.
  3. Re-run show ip bgp <prefix> and confirm attribute and selected path.
  4. Document and prepare rollback commands.

Attribute changes can create asymmetric flows or black-holing. Always test and have a rollback plan.

Route-maps are your safe, auditable mechanism to set attributes. Verify results and prepare to revert if behavior is unexpected.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Best Path Issues
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting BGP best-path issues is methodical: gather all candidate paths, compare attributes in the exact algorithm order, and find which attribute first differs. Start with show ip bgp <network> longer-prefixes to list all available paths and then inspect a specific path with show ip bgp <network> <mask> | begin Path to see attributes such as weight, local-pref, AS path, origin, and MED. Look first for weight and local-preference values because they short-circuit later checks. If those match, compare AS path lengths, then origin, then MED — but remember MED only compares for routes from the same neighbor AS. Another practical tip is to check IGP metrics to the BGP next-hop because the lowest IGP metric to the next-hop is used late in the selection. If you see unexpected behavior, confirm that route-maps or neighbor configurations did not inadvertently set attributes. A useful workflow is to capture the pre-change state, apply the change in a maintenance window, and capture the post-change state so deltas are clear. Always verify on multiple iBGP speakers to confirm whether the change propagated. Finally, maintain a rollback plan: if your modification creates undesirable traffic shifts, revert and analyze in a lab. This structured approach reduces downtime and helps you identify which attribute to modify safely.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how BGP decides which route is best and which attributes you can change to shape traffic. BGP is the protocol that governs how autonomous systems exchange reachability; it does not rely on a single numeric metric like many interior protocols. Instead, it evaluates a sequence of path attributes — including weight, local preference, AS path, origin, MED, and communities — to make deterministic decisions. You'll see that some attributes are local to a router, some are shared inside an AS, and others are exchanged between ASes. This distinction matters because it determines whether you can influence outbound traffic from your AS, or inbound traffic seen by your peers. Concrete examples in the chapter show using a neighbor weight, setting local preference via a route-map, and AS path prepending to alter how an upstream ISP prefers your routes. We'll also cover the exact order BGP evaluates attributes so you avoid common mistakes, like attempting to use MED when local preference already resolved the choice. By the end you'll be able to explain the evaluation order, apply route-maps to set attributes, and reason about the impact of changes on inter-domain routing. Consider how a single attribute change could make a backup link carry all traffic — that's why careful testing matters. Why might you prefer local preference over AS path prepending for outbound traffic control? We'll explore that in detail.

These objectives are designed so you can both explain and act on BGP path behavior. First, you'll identify key BGP path attributes — weight, local preference, AS path, origin, MED, and community — and explain where each one applies. That means distinguishing router-local attributes from those exchanged inside an AS, and those sent between ASes. Second, you'll describe the BGP best path selection algorithm as an ordered decision process so you can predict which attribute will win when two policies conflict. Third, you'll set and test attributes using route-maps to influence outbound and inbound traffic, including configuring neighbor weight and local-preference and performing AS path prepending. Finally, you'll reason about the operational implications and troubleshoot common selection issues using the show ip bgp commands. Each objective combines conceptual knowledge and lab actions so you can prove competency. For example, after learning to set local preference with a route-map you'll test outbound path selection and verify that all iBGP speakers pick the configured exit. Keep in mind that manipulating attributes has safety implications; always validate in a controlled environment and document changes before applying to production.

This second objectives slide turns the concepts into verifiable skills. You should be able to set the neighbor weight and confirm that the local router prefers that path, and likewise set a local-preference with a route-map and validate across iBGP speakers that the same exit is chosen. For inbound traffic shaping, you will configure AS path prepending and then use show ip bgp commands on a peer to confirm the longer AS path is visible. You will also interpret origin codes — IGP, EGP, or Incomplete — and understand when MED comparisons are meaningful, namely only when the competing routes come from the same neighboring AS. Finally, you must be able to run show ip bgp for a prefix and read the attributes to determine which attribute decided the selection. Each skill includes a verification step so you can show that the configuration had the intended effect. Practice in a lab first and document the before-and-after state so you can roll back easily. Successful completion means you can both reason about and reproduce a controlled attribute change and its observed routing effect.

Weight is a Cisco-proprietary attribute that exists only on the local router and is the first criterion in BGP's best path selection. Because weight is evaluated before every other attribute, setting a higher weight on a route immediately makes the local router prefer that route for outbound traffic. This makes weight ideal for quick, per-router overrides where you want a specific speaker to use a chosen exit without affecting other iBGP peers. You can configure weight directly with a neighbor statement or set it in a route-map. For example, using neighbor 10.0.0.2 weight 200 makes routes from that neighbor preferred locally. Alternatively, a route-map applied inbound can match specific prefixes and set weight values selectively. A concrete use case is when a router has two eBGP neighbors and you need one router to prefer the lower-cost link for certain prefixes while leaving other routers unchanged. A common misconception is to use weight when you mean to influence the entire AS; remember weight does not propagate, so it will not change decisions on other routers. Key verification steps are to run show ip bgp for the prefix on the router and observe the weight value and the selected route. Always document weight changes and test in lab because local overrides can cause asymmetric flows that complicate troubleshooting.

Local Preference is a well-known, discretionary attribute that iBGP peers exchange inside an autonomous system. It is evaluated after weight but before AS path, so setting a higher local preference on routes learned from a chosen neighbor causes all iBGP speakers to prefer that exit for outbound traffic. This makes local preference the primary tool when you want entire AS behavior to change, unlike weight which only affects a single router. Typically you set local preference using a route-map applied on inbound neighbor sessions, for example set local-preference 200 for prefixes learned from your preferred upstream. A concrete scenario: if Router A should be the primary exit for 1.1.1.0/24, configure the neighbor connected to Router A to set local preference higher than default 100. Verification involves running show ip bgp for the prefix on multiple iBGP speakers and confirming the local-preference value and that the chosen next-hop aligns with your desired exit. A common misconception is to rely on AS path for outbound control; AS path affects how other ASes prefer your routes for inbound traffic, not how your AS chooses its own exit. Use local preference for AS-wide outbound policy and document the policy so operators understand global path preferences.

AS_Path is a list of autonomous system numbers a route has traversed and is central to how remote ASes decide where to send traffic to you. BGP prefers shorter AS paths, so adding your AS number multiple times — prepending — makes your route appear longer and therefore less preferred by upstream peers. This is the standard operational method to influence inbound traffic without asking your peers to change their policies. For example, if Router Y should be a backup for 203.0.113.0/24, configure Router Y to prepend its AS number two or three times before advertising the prefix to the ISP. The chapter example shows a route-map PREPEND_AS with set as-path prepend 65002 65002 65002 applied outbound. After changes, verify on your peer with show ip bgp that the AS_Path length increased. A common trap is over-prepending: if you add too many AS numbers you may make the route unreachable or cause unexpected failover to a longer but stable path. Also remember AS path only affects other ASes' inbound decisions — it will not change your own AS outbound choices. Think of AS path as advertising a longer road to make others choose a different entrance to reach you.

Origin and MED are attributes that come after AS path in the selection sequence and provide additional tie-breaking information. Origin indicates how the route entered BGP: IGP (marked i) for routes injected via the network command, EGP (deprecated), or Incomplete (?) for redistributed routes. Origin is preferred in the order IGP > EGP > Incomplete, so prefer declaring routes via network where possible to give them higher origin preference. MED, or Multi-Exit Discriminator, is an optional attribute that suggests to a neighboring AS which entry point into your AS it should prefer; lower MED is better. Important nuance: MED comparisons are only meaningful when comparing routes received from the same neighboring AS. If you set MED on routes learned from different ASes, BGP will not compare them unless additional configuration is present. A common mistake is to set MED expecting to influence decisions across different upstreams — because MED is evaluated later and constrained by source neighbor, it often has no effect. Use MED when you and a peer have multiple peering points and you want to influence which of your links they will choose. Verify MED values appearing in show ip bgp output and confirm whether routes compared come from the same neighbor.

BGP community is an optional, transitive attribute used to tag routes so receiving ASes can apply consistent policies. Communities themselves are not part of the core best-path decision sequence, but they are powerful policy levers. Common communities like no-export or no-advertise control where a route is propagated, and custom communities let you mark prefixes for actions such as prepending, blackholing, or special handling by transit partners. For example, you might tag certain prefixes with a community that instructs an upstream to prefer a particular POP or to avoid advertising the prefix beyond their network. Because communities travel across AS boundaries when transitive, they enable coordination between you and your providers. A misconception is assuming communities automatically change route preference; they only carry labels. The peer must be configured to act on those communities. Use route-maps to set communities with set community and document the semantics you expect from each peer. Verify community propagation via show ip bgp and by asking a cooperative peer to confirm the received community tags in their BGP table. Communities are a policy language — use them to make complex operator intent explicit and automatable.

The BGP best path selection algorithm is a strict, ordered list of checks that BGP uses to select one best path among many. Understanding the sequence is essential so you apply the correct attribute when you want to influence selection. The sequence begins with weight — the Cisco-local override — followed by local preference for AS-wide decisions. Next, routes that were originated locally via network or redistribute are preferred. Then BGP considers AS_Path length, favoring the shortest list of AS numbers. After AS path, Origin preference is evaluated with IGP preferred over EGP and Incomplete. MED comes next, but MED is only compared when competing routes come from the same neighbor AS. If still tied, eBGP-learned routes are preferred over iBGP, then the lowest IGP metric to the BGP next-hop. For ties among eBGP routes, BGP prefers the oldest route for stability, then breaks remaining ties using the lowest BGP router ID and finally the lowest neighbor IP address. A common troubleshooting mistake is attempting to change a late-stage attribute like MED when an earlier attribute already decided the winner. When you troubleshoot, gather the full path list with show ip bgp <prefix> longer-prefixes and examine each attribute in the precise order above. This lets you reason why one path was chosen and which attribute you need to change to get a different outcome.
